2027-07-30.title: Fourth Friday of Kaitha
2027-07-30.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The lowly boast in being raised up; the rich will fade like the flower
2027-07-30.alt: Season of Kaitha (Qaita, summer), which began on 4 July with the Feast of the Twelve Apostles: the season of the Church's growth and harvest, when she remembers the apostles and martyrs who watered her with their blood and waits in readiness for the Lord's coming. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari. The calendar's own headings: “Let the lowly brother boast in his exaltation”; “The most important commandments”. The Fridays of Kaitha are kept in memory of the martyrs and saints of the Church (verify locally for today). In the Latin calendar, today is the optional memorial of St Peter Chrysologus, bishop and Doctor of the Church; the Mass readings are Leviticus 23:1, 4–11, 15–16, 27, 34b–37 and Matthew 13:54–58.
2027-07-30.verse: He said to him, “‘You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind.’ This is the greatest and first commandment. And a second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’
theo: On the Friday that closes the fourth week of Kaitha, the Church gives us the shortest reading of the week and one of the most demanding. James writes only three verses, and in them turns the world's scale upside down: “Let the believer who is lowly boast in being raised up, and the rich in being brought low, because the rich will disappear like a flower in the field.” The lowly believer, the one whom the world overlooks, is told to boast, because in Christ he has been raised to the dignity of a child of God. The rich believer is told to boast too, but in being brought low, in the humility of seeing that wealth does not last. James is not praising poverty or condemning money; he is changing the place where we stand to measure our worth. Elsewhere he asks: “Has not God chosen the poor in the world to be rich in faith and to be heirs of the kingdom that he has promised to those who love him?”

The picture he uses is one that every Malayali knows from July: “For the sun rises with its scorching heat and withers the field; its flower falls, and its beauty perishes. It is the same way with the rich; in the midst of a busy life, they will wither away.” After weeks of rain the grass is thick and green, and the flowers are everywhere; then a few days of hot sun in a break of the monsoon, and the tender growth dries and turns brown. So it is with human strength and success. Isaiah says it in the same way: “All people are grass, their constancy is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the Lord blows upon it.” The point is not despair, but relief: what fades should not be the foundation of a life. Jesus puts it simply: “Take care! Be on your guard against all kinds of greed; for one's life does not consist in the abundance of possessions.”

The Gospel gives the foundation that does not fade. Pharisees gather after Jesus has silenced the Sadducees, and one of them, a lawyer, asks him a question to test him: “Teacher, which commandment in the law is the greatest?” Jesus answers from the Scriptures that every devout Jew knew by heart. The first words come from the Shema, the prayer of Israel: “Hear, O Israel: The Lord is our God, the Lord alone. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.” The second comes from Leviticus: “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Jesus is not setting aside the law of Israel; he is showing its centre. This answer belongs to the heart of Jewish faith and is shared with the Church, and it should make us look with respect at the people to whom we owe it.

“On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets.” A door hangs on its hinges, and a garment hangs on its peg; the whole of Scripture hangs on love. The two commandments are one love: the second is “like” the first, and the First Letter of John joins them with an edge: “Those who say, ‘I love God,’ and hate their brothers or sisters, are liars; for those who do not love a brother or sister whom they have seen, cannot love God whom they have not seen.” Paul adds: “Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore, love is the fulfilling of the law.” The rich and the lowly of James's letter are both neighbours to each other, and the love of neighbour is what makes the rich man's fading wealth useful: shared, it becomes a treasure in heaven. Alphonsa, Martha and Joachim and Anne, whom we have remembered this week, each lived these two commandments in their own way.

As Kaitha continues, we are at the heart of the monsoon, and the great rivers are rising. A river does not ask whose compound it is; the water goes where it goes and shows that no human house is the foundation of anything. The only foundation that does not wash away is the love of God and neighbour. The prayer of the Holy Qurbana puts us in this love: we stand before God with the whole heart, and then we turn to give the sign of peace to our neighbour. Let us ask that, on the day when the flower fades and the grass dries, the Lord may find in us what he asked of the lawyer: the love that is the fulfilling of the law.
outline: Three verses that turn the scale upside down: the lowly raised, the rich brought low.
Point 1 · Boast in the right place
The lowly boast in their dignity; the rich in their humility; wealth fades like the flower of the field.
Point 2 · The foundation that does not fade
The lawyer's question; the Shema and Leviticus; the whole of Scripture hangs on love.
Love of God cannot be separated from love of neighbour; shared wealth becomes lasting.
“You shall love the Lord your God… and your neighbor as yourself.”
live: If you feel small, remember your dignity as a child of God; if you feel secure, remember how little of it you will keep. Say a short prayer for each state.
Choose one possession or sum that you can share with a person in need this week, and give it.
Each morning this week, say: “Lord, you alone are God; I love you with my whole heart,” then name one neighbour whom you will love in a concrete way that day.
fathers: Love, and do what you will. If you keep silent, keep silent out of love; if you speak, speak out of love; if you correct, correct out of love; if you spare, spare out of love. Let the root of love be within you, and nothing but good can grow from it.

Why do you take pride in riches, which pass like the flowers of spring? The rich man shines for a short time and then withers; but the one who loves the poor stores up what does not wither. Make your wealth a bridge to heaven by giving it to Christ in the poor.
God gave us two commandments in one: whoever loves God will love his neighbour, because God has commanded it. Whoever loves his neighbour also loves God, to whom the love is offered.
magis: When someone asks Jesus which commandment in the Law is the greatest, he replies: you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind; the second is like it: you shall love your neighbour as yourself.
In response to the question about the first of the commandments, Jesus says: the love of God and the love of neighbour are inseparable; on these two commandments hang the whole law and the prophets.
God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor and rebukes those who turn away from them; love for the poor is incompatible with immoderate love of riches or their selfish use.
saints: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. In the Latin calendar, the optional memorial of St Peter Chrysologus, bishop and Doctor of the Church (about 380–450), known for his short and loving sermons.

25–31 July: the fourth week of the Season of Kaitha. Sun 25: Fourth Sunday of Kaitha (St James the Apostle gives way to the Sunday; World Day for Grandparents and the Elderly). Mon 26: Sts Joachim and Anne, the parents of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Wed 28: St Alphonsa, the first woman of Indian origin to be canonised, an important feast. Thu 29: St Martha. Fri 30: Fourth Friday of Kaitha. Sat 31: St Ignatius of Loyola. In the Latin calendar the same days keep Sts Joachim and Anne (26), St Alphonsa (28, a memorial in India), Sts Martha, Mary and Lazarus (29) and St Ignatius (31). Looking ahead: the month of August and the later weeks of Kaitha.
2027-07-30.prayer: Lord God, you alone are God, and you ask us to love you with our whole heart and our neighbour as ourselves. Teach us to measure our lives by your love and not by what fades. Raise up those who are lowly and teach the rich to be humble, so that all may boast in you. When the sun scorches and the flower falls, let us stand on the one foundation that does not wash away. Make our homes and our parishes places where the love of God and neighbour is one love. Through the prayers of your martyrs and saints, whom we remember in these days of Kaitha, keep us in your love. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana the two commandments become one action. With our whole heart we offer ourselves to God, and then we turn to our neighbour with the sign of peace. The Bread of life is the love of God made flesh, and whoever receives it is sent to love in the same way.

quick: James: the lowly may boast in being raised up; the rich must be brought low, for they will fade like the flower of the field.
Matthew: the lawyer's question; Jesus answers with the love of God and the love of neighbour, on which hang the whole law and the prophets.
Both: only love lasts; wealth and success fade like grass.
2027-07-30.action: Give something away this week that you would normally keep, and say the Shema each morning.
2027-07-30.question: What am I building my life on: something that will fade like the flower, or the love of God and neighbour?

family.explain: A man asked Jesus, ‘Teacher, which is the greatest of all God's commands?’ Jesus said, ‘Love the Lord your God with all your heart. And the second is like it: love your neighbour as yourself.’ When we love God and our neighbour, we keep everything God asks. James says that money and fine things are like a flower in the field: pretty for a while, and then gone. But love never goes away.
family.intention: We pray for people who are poor and for people who have much, that all may share and love.
family.ask: Ask: “Who is our neighbour this week? What can we share with them?”

illus: One year in the heavy monsoon (a story told to illustrate the reading) the water rose in a village near Alappuzha. The richest man in the village had a big compound and a car, and his gate was locked, because he was afraid of thieves. When the water came up to the veranda, his car stalled in the road, and the only man who came to push it was Kunjan, the coconut-climber, whom he had underpaid for years. Standing waist-deep in the water the rich man said, ‘Kunjan, why do you help me?’ Kunjan answered, ‘Saar, the water does not ask whose house it is. Why should I?’ When the water went down, the rich man paid Kunjan all the wages he owed, and opened the gate. He told the vicar later: ‘That day I learned that my wealth could float away like a leaf.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you gave us the greatest commandment. Gather us now in your love; teach us to love God with all our heart and our neighbour as ourselves. Amen.
share: Let the believer who is lowly boast in being raised up (James 1:9). How do I see my dignity as a child of God?
The rich will disappear like a flower in the field (James 1:10). What do I trust more than God?
You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart (Matthew 22:37). Is God first in my day?
You shall love your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 22:39). Whom do I find hardest to love?
interc: For the Church, that she may be known by love of God and neighbour.
For the poor and the lowly, that they may know their dignity and be helped.
For the rich and powerful, that they may be humble and generous.
For those hit by the monsoon floods and landslides, that they may find help and shelter.
For all whom we find hard to love, that God may bless them and us.
pm.close: Father, your Son taught us that love is the fulfilment of the law. Pour your love into our hearts and keep us in it until the day when the flower fades and your kingdom comes. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, the Gospel today has a simple question and a simple answer. A lawyer asks Jesus, “Teacher, which commandment in the law is the greatest?” (Matthew 22:36). Jesus answers with two sentences from the Bible that every Jewish child knew: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the greatest and first commandment. And a second is like it: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Matthew 22:37–39).

“On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets” (Matthew 22:40). Think of a door: it hangs on its hinge. Think of a garment: it hangs on a peg. The whole Bible hangs on love. If we have love, we have the whole of what God asks. If we have no love, all the rest is empty. And these two commandments cannot be separated. Saint John says: “Those who say, ‘I love God,’ and hate their brothers or sisters, are liars” (1 John 4:20).

The reading from the letter of James is only three verses. Saint James says: “Let the believer who is lowly boast in being raised up, and the rich in being brought low, because the rich will disappear like a flower in the field” (James 1:9–10). The poor person, whom the world forgets, has the dignity of a child of God. The rich person must remember that money is like grass: green for a season, and then dried by the sun.

We see this in July. After the heavy rain the grass is green and thick, and then the sun comes out in a break of the monsoon, and it begins to dry. Our strength, our money, our position are like that. They are gifts, but they do not last. What lasts is love. And love is not only a feeling; it is a decision to give: time to an old person, food to a hungry neighbour, patience to someone difficult.

In these days we have remembered Saint Alphonsa, Saint Martha, and the grandparents of Jesus. Each of them lived this one commandment in their own way. This week, let us build on the one foundation that does not wash away: love of God and love of neighbour. Amen.
kids: Children, someone asked Jesus: what is the most important thing God wants? And Jesus said: love God with all your heart, and love other people like yourself. If you remember only this, you remember everything! This week, say to God every morning: ‘I love you.’ And share something with a friend or your brother or sister. That is how we keep God's greatest commandment!

concl: Everything that is gathered in our hands fades like grass; the love of God and neighbour is the one thing that stays.
The whole of Scripture hangs on it.
2027-07-30.resolve: This week, say the Shema each morning, share one possession, and love one hard neighbour in a concrete way.
